title: Markets & the Economy
promise: Interest rates, inflation, jobs and growth: the tide that lifts or sinks every boat.
unlock: See why interest rates move every market
Work out your real return after inflation
Spot the big release days on the economic calendar
Know which sectors tend to lead in each phase of the cycle
Tell news from noise, and spot what’s already priced in

questions.q: Traders expected a rate cut of 0.25 points. The central bank cuts 0.50 points. How do stocks often react?
options: Often up: money got cheaper than expected
Often down: lower rates make cash pay more
Little move: a cut was expected anyway
questions.why: The surprise moves prices. A cut twice the size traders expected makes money cheaper than they priced in, so stocks often rise.
questions.work: Expected cut 0.25 points. Actual cut 0.50 points. A 0.25-point surprise.

questions.q: Your savings pay 2% a year. Inflation is 6%. What is your real return?
questions.why: Inflation is taken away, not added. You earn 2%, but prices rise 6%.
questions.work: 2% − 6% ≈ −4%. $10,000 earns $200, but the same goods cost $600 more.

questions.q: The jobs report lands at 8:30 tomorrow. You hold your normal size, with a stop very close to price. What could happen at 8:30?

chart.label: One-minute candles creep up toward 8:30 with a stop just below price

options: Price may jump past your stop, so it fills at a worse price
Your stop always fills at its exact price
Nothing: trading is calm around big releases
questions.why: At a big release price can jump in a second. A stop becomes a market order, so it fills at the next price available, which can be worse.

questions.q: The economy is past its low and starting to grow again. Which sector has often led in this phase?
questions.why: In an early recovery, banks, tech and shops have often led as demand comes back. Staples and utilities tend to shine in slowdowns.

questions.q: Headline: “Company profit up 30%.” Analysts had expected +30% for weeks. The stock barely moves. Why?
questions.why: Everyone expected +30% for weeks, so the price had already moved. With no surprise, there was little left to move.

retry.q: Traders expected a rate cut of 0.25 points. The central bank holds rates instead. How do stocks often react?
options: Often down: money stayed costlier than hoped
Often up: no change is good news
retry.why: The cut traders priced in didn’t come, so money stays costlier than expected. Stocks often fall on the day.
retry.work: Expected cut 0.25 points. Actual: no cut. A 0.25-point surprise.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy

retry.q: A bond pays 5% a year. Inflation is 2%. What is your real return?
retry.why: Take inflation away from what you earn. The bond beats inflation, so your buying power grows.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy

retry.q: You hold twice your normal size. CPI comes out Wednesday at 8:30 and the jobs report Friday at 8:30. What’s the sensible plan?
options: Cut size before Wednesday and Friday
Remove your stops for the week
retry.why: High-impact releases can jump price either way. A smaller size keeps a bad jump to a loss you can live with.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy

retry.q: Growth is slowing toward a recession. Which pair of sectors has often held up best?
retry.why: People keep buying basics and paying for power and water, so staples and utilities often hold up in a slowdown.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy

retry.q: Analysts expected profit up 20%. The company reports +10%. The stock falls 7%. Why?
retry.why: The price had been set for +20%. Growth still disappoints when it’s less good than hoped.
retry.added: Retry question written for the Academy

refresher.title: Lesson 1 · Interest rates move everything
refresher.text: Markets price in the rate they expect. The surprise moves stocks: a bigger cut than expected often lifts them, a surprise hike or a missing cut often sinks them.

refresher.title: Lesson 2 · Inflation and your money
refresher.text: Real return = return − inflation. Savings at 2% with 6% inflation means about −4%: your money buys less.

refresher.title: Lesson 3 · The economic calendar
refresher.text: Around big releases price can jump either way in seconds, and stops can fill at worse prices. Check the calendar and size down before high-impact days.

refresher.title: Lesson 4 · Sectors and the cycle
refresher.text: Early recovery: banks, tech and shops have often led. Late expansion: energy. Slowdown and recession: staples and utilities often hold up. Tendencies, not rules.

refresher.title: Lesson 5 · News vs noise
refresher.text: Prices move on the surprise, not the headline. If the news was expected, it’s already priced in.
